glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 1 states the book’s purpose and its motto, that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, and then sets two voices before a young man: sinners who invite him into violent greed, and Wisdom, who calls him to turn and live.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Solomon’s name heads the book (1:1), though later headings name other wise men as well. A father, honoring the mother’s teaching beside his own, prepares his son for the voices he will meet in the streets.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, But fools despise wisdom and instruction.” (Proverbs 1:7)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 1 is the doorway to the whole book. It offers wisdom, the skill of living life God’s way, along with instruction, prudence, and wise counsel (1:2–5). It is written for “the simple” and “the young man,” yet “A wise man will hear and increase learning” (1:4–5). Then comes the motto that governs everything after it: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). The fear of the LORD is a right view of God, and once God is seen rightly, everything else can begin to be seen rightly. Fools despise this instruction because their trouble lies in the will, not the mind.

The rest of the chapter sets two voices side by side. A gang of sinners offers the son belonging and easy money, “Let us all have one purse” (1:14), but the father shows that they “lie in wait for their own blood” (1:18). Then Wisdom raises her voice at the city gates, calling the simple, the scorners, and the fools to turn, and warning that those who refuse “shall eat the fruit of their own way” (1:31). The poem pictures Wisdom as a woman calling in public. In the fuller light of the New Testament, this is the voice of Christ, “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), who still calls people to turn and live.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 1:1–7 — The Purpose of Proverbs and the Fear of the LORD

The book names Solomon and states its aim: to give wisdom, instruction, and discernment to the simple, the young, and even the wise, and to train readers to search out the riddles of the wise. The introduction closes with the motto of the whole book, that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, while fools despise wisdom and instruction.

Proverbs 1:8–9 — Hear Your Father and Mother

A father calls his son to hear his instruction and not to forsake his mother’s teaching. What the son receives at home becomes his honor, like a graceful ornament on his head and chains about his neck.

Proverbs 1:10–19 — Refuse the Enticement of Sinners

The father voices the gang’s invitation to ambush the innocent and share the spoil, so that his son will recognize it, and he answers it with a firm “Do not consent.” Their violence will turn back on them, because greed “takes away the life of its owners” (1:19).

Proverbs 1:20–23 — Wisdom Calls the Simple to Turn

Wisdom cries out in the busiest public places, asking how long the simple will love simplicity, the scorners their scorning, and the fools their hatred of knowledge. To all who turn at her rebuke she promises to pour out her spirit and make her words known, wording that anticipates the LORD’s later promise to pour out His Spirit (Joel 2:28).

Proverbs 1:24–33 — The End of Refusing Wisdom

Because they refused her call and despised her correction, Wisdom will not answer when calamity comes, and they will reap the fruit of their own choices. The chapter ends with two outcomes: the turning away of the simple will slay them, but whoever listens to Wisdom “will dwell safely” (1:33).

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 1 lays the foundation for reading the whole book. Because wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD, the practical counsel that follows about money, speech, work, and family is never mere self-improvement; it is life lived with a right view of God. The sayings ahead describe how God’s world generally works, and they are read as wisdom rather than as promises for every case.

The chapter also shows how people are lost. The gang appeals to belonging and quick gain, and the greatest danger for the simple is drift: “the turning away of the simple will slay them” (1:32). Wisdom’s warning is severe, yet she speaks it while she is still calling, and the Lord behind her call is “not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The fear of the LORD. A right view of God is the beginning of knowledge, and refusing to choose it lies at the root of ruin (1:7, 29).

Two voices and two ways. Sinners and Wisdom both call to the son, and each path leads to its own end (1:10–19, 20–33).

Listening and correction. The wise hear and increase learning, while fools despise instruction and refuse rebuke (1:5, 7, 23–25, 30).

Greed that destroys itself. The violence the gang plans for others returns on its own members (1:11–19).

Wisdom’s public call. Wisdom speaks in the streets and gates where ordinary life is lived, and her call is urgent because the time to answer does not last forever (1:20–28).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Wisdom (1:2, 20). Skill for living life God’s way in every area. In 1:20–33 Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling in public; the New Testament reveals Christ as “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

Proverb (1:1, 6). A short, memorable saying that expresses a practical truth, often by comparison. Proverbs state what is generally true in God’s world, not guarantees for every case.

The fear of the LORD (1:7). A right view of God. For those who defy Him it means terror, and for all it means awe at His glory, majesty, and holiness, for He is unlike any other. It is the “beginning” of knowledge, both its starting point and its chief part.

The simple (1:4, 22, 32). People who are uncommitted and easily led. The book is written to give them prudence, but their drift becomes deadly if they never turn.

Scorners and fools (1:22). Scorners delight in mocking correction, and fools hate knowledge. Both reject wisdom by choice rather than by lack of ability.

Sheol and the Pit (1:12). Names for the grave and the realm of the dead. The gang boasts that it will swallow its victims like the grave itself.

sections.title: The Purpose of Proverbs and the Fear of the LORD
Wisdom Calls the Simple to Turn

1.brief: The book opens under the name of Solomon, the son of David and king of Israel, the king to whom God gave wisdom. This heading introduces the collection that follows, though later headings show that other wise men also contributed to the book.
1.explain:
“The proverbs of Solomon”

The book opens with a title that tells the reader what kind of writing follows and whose name stands over it. A proverb is a short, memorable saying that states a practical truth about life, often by setting one thing beside another for comparison. Such sayings describe how God’s world generally works; they are meant to be weighed and lived, not treated as promises that guarantee an outcome in every case. Solomon’s name stands first because the LORD gave him wisdom in answer to his prayer for “an understanding heart” (1 Kings 3:9), and Scripture says he “spoke three thousand proverbs” (1 Kings 4:32). This heading introduces the whole book, yet later headings name other contributors as well: the wise (22:17; 24:23), Agur (30:1), and King Lemuel (31:1). The book is best described as the wisdom of Solomon and other wise men gathered under his name.

“the son of David, king of Israel:”

These titles anchor the book in Israel’s history. Solomon was David’s son and heir, king over all Israel in the years of peace and plenty before the kingdom divided. A king who had received his own father’s charge now passes wisdom on in a father’s voice, which suits the “my son” addresses that run through chapters 1–9. As son of David, king of peace, and builder of the temple, Solomon also points beyond himself. Jesus, the greater Son of David, said of Himself, “indeed a greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Scripture also records that Solomon’s heart later turned after other gods (1 Kings 11:4). That sober fact does not weaken his proverbs, since their wisdom comes from God, but it shows that possessing wisdom and walking in it are not the same thing.
1.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “proverbs” covers more than short sayings. It can describe a brief maxim, a byword, a parable or comparison, a poem, and even a prophet’s mocking song, which Isaiah calls a “proverb against the king of Babylon” (Isaiah 14:4). That range explains why the title stands over the longer poems of chapters 1–9 as well as over the short sayings that follow.

Solomon’s name appears again in the headings at 10:1 and 25:1. The second of these adds that the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied further proverbs of Solomon, so the book reached its final form no earlier than Hezekiah’s reign.

2.brief: The first purpose of the book is that its readers come to know wisdom, the skill of living life God’s way, together with the instruction that trains it. It also aims to sharpen discernment, so that a person can perceive and weigh the words of understanding he hears.
2.explain:
The lines of 1:2–6 form one long purpose statement, with line after line opening with “To.” Before a single proverb is given, the reader is told what the book is meant to accomplish in him.

“To know wisdom and instruction,”

Wisdom in Proverbs is skill for living life God’s way: knowing what to do, how to do it, and why, and then doing it in speech, work, money, marriage, and worship. To know it means more than collecting information about it; it means becoming acquainted with it in practice. Beside wisdom stands instruction, the training and correction that discipline a life. The two belong together, for no one becomes skilled at living without being taught and corrected along the way. Proverbs 1:7 will name exactly this pair as what fools despise.

“To perceive the words of understanding,”

To perceive is to discern, to tell one thing from another. Words of understanding are sayings that carry insight, and the book wants its readers able to weigh what they hear. That skill is tested before the chapter ends, when the smooth pitch of violent men and the public cry of Wisdom compete for the same young man. A person who cannot tell those voices apart will usually follow the louder or more attractive one.
2.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “instruction” means training and discipline, and it includes correction. Proverbs uses the same word for “the chastening of the LORD” in 3:11, so the instruction this book offers corrects as well as informs.

The Hebrew word for “wisdom” is also used for practical skill. When the LORD filled Bezalel “with the Spirit of God, in wisdom” for the work of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3), the word described the skill of a craftsman.

3.brief: Proverbs wants its readers to receive the instruction of wisdom as a disciplined way of life, and it names the fruit that follows: justice, judgment, and equity. The skill it teaches is moral as well as practical, showing a person how to do what is right and fair toward God and neighbor.
3.explain:
“To receive the instruction of wisdom,”

To receive is to take in what someone else hands over. Wisdom does not rise up from within a person’s own resources; it is received. The phrase translated instruction of wisdom describes training in wise and prudent conduct, the kind of insight that knows how to act well in real situations. The book assumes a learner who is willing to be taught and to accept discipline, an attitude that the next verses describe as the mark of the wise.

“Justice, judgment, and equity;”

Here the book names the fruit of that training. Justice is what is right by God’s standard; judgment is right decision, the fair verdict that settles a matter; equity is straightness, fair dealing with no hidden crookedness. Together they show that the skill Proverbs teaches is moral as well as practical. A person cannot be wise in the book’s sense and crooked at the same time. The point becomes sharp within a few verses, when a gang proposes to ambush “the innocent without cause” (1:11), the very opposite of justice, judgment, and equity.
3.notes:
The Hebrew word behind “wisdom” in this verse is not the word for wisdom used in 1:2. It comes from a verb meaning to act prudently or with insight, and it describes the good sense that knows how to act well and succeed. ESV renders the phrase instruction in “wise dealing,” and NASB instruction in “wise behavior.”

NKJV’s “Justice” translates the Hebrew noun usually rendered “righteousness,” and ESV and NASB begin the list with “righteousness.” The same three Hebrew nouns return together in 2:9, where NKJV translates them “righteousness and justice, Equity.” There they describe what the son who seeks wisdom will come to understand, so the purpose stated here is the result promised there.

4.brief: The book is written for the simple, those who are uncommitted and easily led, to give them prudence, the good sense to see danger coming. It also gives the young man knowledge and discretion as he steps into life, so the inexperienced need not learn everything through painful mistakes.
4.explain:
“To give prudence to the simple,”

The book is written first for the simple. In Proverbs the simple person is not unintelligent; he is uncommitted, open in every direction, without settled convictions, and so easily led. He is not yet set against wisdom, but he is not yet committed to it either. Proverbs means to give him prudence, the good sense to see danger coming and act on it. A later saying describes this exactly: “A prudent man foresees evil and hides himself, But the simple pass on and are punished” (22:3). The book starts with the person most at risk, which shows the generosity of its purpose.

“To the young man knowledge and discretion—”

The young man stands at the threshold of adult life, where choices about companions, money, work, and sexuality begin to set the direction of everything after. He is offered knowledge and discretion, the ability to think ahead and plan with purpose. Instruction received in advance spares him from having to learn every lesson through painful mistakes. The opening chapters are full of exactly such forewarning, beginning with the scene in 1:10–19.
4.notes:
The Hebrew word for “simple” comes from a verb meaning to be open or easily persuaded, and that same verb is translated “entice” in 1:10. The simple are, by the very name Proverbs gives them, the people sinners set out to entice.

The Hebrew noun translated “prudence” comes from the same root as the adjective rendered “prudent” in 22:3, a root meaning to be shrewd. That adjective can describe crafty cunning, as with the serpent in Genesis 3:1, where NKJV renders it “cunning.” Proverbs uses these words in their good sense, for the practical shrewdness that sees danger coming.

5.brief: Proverbs is not only for beginners, for a wise man will listen and keep adding to what he knows, and a man of understanding will gain wise counsel. A teachable spirit marks the wise, and the wiser a person becomes, the more he wants to hear.
5.explain:
“A wise man will hear and increase learning,”

The purpose statement pauses to say that Proverbs is not only for beginners. The first thing said of the wise man is that he hears. Teachability, not intelligence, is what separates him from the fool of 1:7. Wisdom does not end learning; it adds to it, so that the more a person grows wise, the more he wants to hear. A later verse makes the same point: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser” (9:9). The Hebrew word translated learning is related to the verb behind “To receive” in 1:3; it describes teaching that a person takes in and makes his own.

“And a man of understanding will attain wise counsel,”

The man of understanding does not rely on his own insight alone. He gains wise counsel, the kind of guidance needed to steer decisions well. Proverbs repeatedly connects good outcomes with good counsel and failure with going alone: “Where there is no counsel, the people fall” (11:14). A person who has understanding is the very one who knows he still needs direction, and he seeks it out.
5.notes: “Wise counsel” translates a Hebrew word for guidance in making plans. It always appears in the plural and only in the wisdom books, and it is used for the planning needed to wage war (20:18; 24:6). The word has often been connected with ropes and the steering of a ship, which would picture counsel as the skill of steering a course, though that origin is not certain.

6.brief: The book also trains its readers to understand a proverb and an enigma, the sayings and riddles of the wise. Some sayings carry meaning beneath their surface, and the reader is called to search them out rather than skim them.
6.explain:
“To understand a proverb and an enigma,”

The purpose statement resumes. A proverb, as in 1:1, is a short saying that states a truth, often by comparison. An enigma is a saying whose meaning is not on the surface and must be worked out. Some proverbs are plain at first hearing; others yield their meaning only to a reader who stops, turns them over, and thinks. The book means to train that kind of reader.

“The words of the wise and their riddles.”

The words of the wise are the sayings of Israel’s teachers, and later headings in the book use the same description for whole collections (22:17; 24:23). Riddles are sayings with a hidden meaning that has to be searched out. The book itself praises such searching: “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter, But the glory of kings is to search out a matter” (25:2). This verse is part of the ground for the deeper, layered readings that Proverbs supports at certain points, such as Wisdom’s banquet in chapter 9 and the woman of valor in chapter 31. Such readings always come after the plain meaning and never replace it.
6.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “enigma” is paired with the word for “proverb” again in Habakkuk 2:6, where NKJV renders it “taunting riddle.”

The Hebrew word for “riddles” is the word used of Samson’s riddle in Judges 14:12 and of the “hard questions” with which the queen of Sheba came to test Solomon in 1 Kings 10:1. In both stories the meaning had to be worked out by someone with insight.

7.brief: Here is the motto of the whole book: the fear of the LORD, a right view of God, is the beginning of knowledge, both its starting point and its chief part. Fools despise wisdom and instruction, which shows that their problem is a refusal to bow before God and receive correction, not a lack of intelligence.
7.explain:
“The fear of the LORD”

Here is the motto of the whole book. The fear of the LORD is a right view of God. LORD translates the personal name by which God revealed Himself to Israel, so the wisdom of Proverbs rests on knowing the God who made Himself known, not on human observation alone. How this fear is expressed depends on where a person stands. For those who defy God it rightly includes terror; for all who see Him it means awe at His glory, majesty, and holiness, for He is unlike any other. This fear is never mere respect, yet it does not drive the humble away. The God who is feared is good, and a right view of Him draws people near.

“is the beginning of knowledge,”

Beginning means both the starting point and the chief or foremost part. Knowledge starts with the fear of the LORD, and the fear of the LORD remains its most important element. Once God is seen rightly, everything else can begin to be seen rightly: oneself, other people, money, work, pleasure, and death. A person may be brilliant and still not know anything rightly if he leaves God out.

“But fools despise wisdom and instruction.”

The second line gives the contrast. The fool in Proverbs is not someone lacking intelligence but someone morally resistant. He despises, treating with contempt what he ought to receive. What he despises is the very pair named in 1:2, wisdom and instruction, so the purpose statement ends where it began. The fool’s problem is a refusal to bow before God and accept correction. The motto recurs at key points in the book (9:10; 15:33), and the final portrait honors “a woman who fears the LORD” (31:30).
7.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “beginning” is the word used for “firstfruits” in 3:9, the first and best portion of the harvest. That use supports the sense of foremost as well as first. The related saying in 9:10, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom,” uses a different Hebrew word that stresses the starting point.

NKJV’s “fools” in this verse and in 1:22 translates two different Hebrew words. Proverbs has several words for the fool, and the difference cannot be seen in English. In both verses the fool is identified by his attitude toward truth: here he despises wisdom and instruction, and in 1:22 he hates knowledge.

The same conviction appears outside Proverbs in nearly the same words: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 111:10), and “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” (Job 28:28).

8.brief: A father now begins speaking to his son, and he sets the mother’s teaching beside his own: “My son, hear the instruction of your father.” The son is to listen to his father and not abandon what his mother has taught him, for wisdom is first handed down in the home.
8.explain:
“My son,”

With these words a new voice begins, and it will speak through most of chapters 1–9. It is a real father preparing a young man for life, using the warm address “My son” again and again. The address later widens to “my children” (7:24), so every reader who listens may hear himself addressed. The father’s voice also carries God’s own fatherly care as He instructs His children, for Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes the similar address of 3:11–12 as God’s word to believers.

“hear the instruction of your father,”

To hear in this sense is to listen with the intention of obeying. The father’s instruction is the same discipline named in 1:2 and 1:7, the training that wise people receive and fools despise. The son’s first task is not to work out wisdom for himself but to listen to someone who has walked further down the road.

“And do not forsake the law of your mother;”

The mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s, and both parents are honored (compare 6:20; 31:1). Law here means teaching or direction, the guidance she has given her son. To forsake is to abandon or let go. Wisdom is first handed down in the home, from parents who teach their children as they live together, as Israel was commanded: “You shall teach them diligently to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:7).
8.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “law” is torah, the word Israel used for the Law of Moses, but its basic sense is instruction or direction. Proverbs uses it of the mother’s teaching here and in 6:20, and of the woman of valor’s speech in 31:26, “the law of kindness.”

Other ancient wisdom writings were framed the same way. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, for example, is presented as a father’s teaching to his son, so the form of these chapters would have been familiar to their first hearers.

9.brief: Parental instruction is pictured as a graceful ornament on the head and chains about the neck, signs of honor and beauty. A son who keeps what he was taught wears it openly, and his life displays the dignity his parents’ wisdom gives him.
9.explain:
“For they will be a graceful ornament on your head,”

“For” introduces the reason to listen. The parents’ teaching is pictured as a graceful ornament, a garland or wreath worn on the head at times of honor and celebration. What the son has been taught does not stay hidden; he wears it, and others see the dignity it gives him. Instruction that may feel like restriction to a young man turns out to be his crowning honor.

“And chains about your neck.”

Chains here are necklaces, ornaments of honor. When Pharaoh raised Joseph to authority, he “put a gold chain around his neck” (Genesis 41:42). The picture is of a life that displays its upbringing well. The contrast with the next scene is deliberate: the gang will offer the son spoil and a share in their purse (1:13–14), but the true adornment of his life is the wisdom his father and mother gave him.
9.notes: The same ornament reappears in 4:9, where Wisdom “will place on your head an ornament of grace.” Proverbs 3:3 and 6:21 also speak of binding wise teaching around the neck.

10.brief: The father’s first warning concerns companions. When sinners try to entice the son, the answer is short and firm, “Do not consent,” with no room left for negotiation.
10.explain:
“My son, if sinners entice you,”

The father’s first warning concerns companions. The sinners here are not people who occasionally stumble; they are men whose way of life is set on wrongdoing, and the next verses show them to be a violent gang. They do not force the son; they entice him. Their method is persuasion, and their target is the simple young man whose heart is open to whatever voice reaches it first. The father assumes that this pressure will come. The question is not whether his son will be tempted but how he will answer.

“Do not consent.”

The answer is short and absolute. In Hebrew it is only two words. The father does not tell his son to listen to the offer, weigh its benefits, and then decide; he tells him to refuse before the conversation goes any further. To consent is to be willing, to give inward agreement. Temptation requires the son’s agreement to succeed, so the responsibility rests with him. A firm no at the beginning spares him from being argued step by step into something he would never have chosen at the outset.
10.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “consent” means to be willing. The same verb returns in 1:25 and 1:30, where those who refuse Wisdom “would have none” of her rebuke and counsel. The son is told not to be willing toward sinners; the scoffers are not willing toward Wisdom.

11.brief: The father voices the gang’s own pitch so the son will recognize it: “Come with us,” they say, inviting him to ambush and murder the innocent without cause. Their appeal begins with belonging and only then reveals the violence behind it.
11.explain:
“Come with us,”

The words begin, “If they say,” and the father now voices the gang’s own words so that his son will recognize them when he hears them. Their pitch opens with belonging: “Come with us.” Before any crime is named, the young man is offered a place in a group. That is often how the path of sin begins, with an appeal to friendship and acceptance that makes the wrong itself seem secondary.

“Let us lie in wait to shed blood;”

Then the plan comes out. To lie in wait is to set an ambush. The gang intends robbery with murder, the kind of highway violence that threatened travelers in ancient Israel. In the days of the judges, the men of Shechem “set men in ambush against him on the tops of the mountains, and they robbed all who passed by them” (Judges 9:25). The gang speaks of shedding blood as casually as if it were an ordinary day’s work.

“Let us lurk secretly for the innocent without cause;”

To lurk secretly is to hide and wait for a victim. Their targets are innocent people who have done them no harm, and the attack is without cause, wholly unprovoked. The words expose what the offer of friendship concealed. Joining these companions means joining in the shedding of innocent blood.
11.notes: The Hebrew word translated “without cause” means for nothing or for no reason. It can be read with the ambush (attacking for no reason) or with the victims (people who have given no reason to be attacked), and the sense is much the same either way.

12.brief: The gang boasts that they will swallow their victims alive and whole, like Sheol, the grave, and like those who go down to the Pit. They speak as if they held the power of death itself, which shows how cruel and arrogant their plan really is.
12.explain:
“Let us swallow them alive like Sheol,”

Sheol is the Hebrew name for the grave, the realm of the dead. Scripture pictures it as a mouth that swallows and is never full. The gang boasts that they will be like Sheol itself, swallowing their victims alive. The words recall the judgment on Korah’s company, when the earth opened and they “went down alive into the pit” (Numbers 16:33). These men speak as if they held the power of death in their own hands.

“And whole, like those who go down to the Pit;”

The Pit stands in parallel with Sheol, another name for the grave. To swallow victims whole is to leave nothing behind. The boast is meant to sound bold and fearless, the kind of talk that can impress a young man who wants to feel strong. The father lets the gang speak in full so that their arrogance and cruelty become plain. Their talk of death will come back on them, for their own lives are what they are really putting at risk (1:18).
12.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “whole” means complete, and NKJV renders the same word “blameless” in 2:21. Here it describes the victims swallowed entire, and it may also hint that they are blameless people, like “the innocent” of 1:11.

In Numbers 16:30 and 16:33 the word NKJV renders “pit” is the Hebrew word Sheol, the same word used here for the grave, the realm of the dead.

13.brief: Their real motive comes out: plunder. They promise all kinds of precious possessions and houses filled with spoil, making violent gain sound like quick and easy wealth, and the riches become the bait meant to draw the young man in.
13.explain:
“We shall find all kinds of precious possessions,”

The real motive now appears: wealth. The gang promises every sort of valuable thing. Murder is presented as a shortcut to riches, and the reward is described in glowing terms while the bloodshed fades into the background. The bait is the young man’s desire for quick and easy gain.

“We shall fill our houses with spoil;”

Spoil is plunder, what is stripped from victims or taken in war. The gang pictures homes filled with stolen goods. Proverbs will say much about houses and what fills them. Here the house is filled by violence, and a later saying warns that “He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house” (15:27). The riches promised are real enough in the short term, which is what makes the offer tempting; the father’s answer will be that such riches cost the lives of those who take them (1:19).

14.brief: The pitch closes with an offer of partnership: cast your lot with us and share one purse. Belonging and an equal share of the profits are held out to a young man who wants both, but joining the gang would mean sharing its guilt and its end.
14.explain:
“Cast in your lot among us,”

Casting lots was a common way of making decisions and dividing property in Israel. To cast in one’s lot with others is to join them and share their fortune, whatever it may be. The gang offers the young man full membership. He will no longer stand outside wondering whether he belongs; he will be one of them.

“Let us all have one purse”—

The purse is the common bag that holds the takings. One purse means an equal share for every member, and that promise is attractive to a young man who has little of his own. Belonging and fairness are both offered, though only among thieves and at the expense of innocent victims. The offer hides its real cost. To share the gang’s purse is to share its guilt and its end, and the father will show that the end is death (1:18–19). The dash at the end of the verse marks the moment the father breaks off the gang’s speech and speaks to his son directly.
14.notes:
The Hebrew word for “purse” is the word used for the merchant’s bag of weights in 16:11, “All the weights in the bag are His work.” There the bag holds honest weights that belong to the LORD; here it holds the takings of robbery.

The lot appears again in 16:33, “The lot is cast into the lap, But its every decision is from the LORD.”

15.brief: Speaking again directly as a father to “My son,” he gives his command: do not walk in the way with them, and keep your foot off their path. Here the book first uses its picture of life as a road, and refusing sin starts with refusing the first step.
15.explain:
“My son, do not walk in the way with them,”

The father breaks into the gang’s speech with his own voice and the tender address “My son.” His command uses the book’s central picture for the first time: life is a way, a road a person walks. To walk in the way with someone is to share his course of life and arrive where he arrives. The father does not merely forbid one crime; he forbids taking the road on which such crimes are done.

“Keep your foot from their path;”

The command becomes concrete. The son is to hold back his own foot. Refusing sin begins with refusing the first step, before the momentum of the group carries him along. The image is simple enough for a young man to remember at the very moment the gang says, “Come with us” (1:11). Proverbs will return to the two ways again and again, and here it begins with a single step held back.

16.brief: The father gives his reason: their feet run to evil, and they hurry to shed blood. The gang’s eagerness exposes where their path leads, and a son who walks with them will be swept along at their pace.
16.explain:
“For their feet run to evil,”

“For” gives the reason behind the command. The son is to keep his foot from their path because their feet run to evil. The contrast is pointed: one foot held back, many feet running. The gang is not drifting into wrongdoing; they are eager for it. A young man who walks with them will not be allowed to set his own pace.

“And they make haste to shed blood.”

Their eagerness reaches its goal in bloodshed. They hurry to do what should make any person stop and tremble. The haste exposes the true direction of their path, and it is also a warning, since people in a hurry do not stop to consider where they are going. The father wants his son to see the destination before he takes the first step. Among the seven things the LORD hates are “Feet that are swift in running to evil” (6:18).
16.notes:
Isaiah 59:7 contains nearly the same words: “Their feet run to evil, And they make haste to shed innocent blood.” Paul quotes the Isaiah wording in Romans 3:15.

The NET Bible’s textual note reports that this verse does not appear in Codex B (Codex Vaticanus), an important manuscript of the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, or in the Coptic and Arabic versions. The same note judges that the verse fits its context well enough to be original. It stands in the Hebrew text, and NKJV and other major English versions include it.

17.brief: A picture from bird-catching follows: spreading a net where the bird can see it is wasted effort. The image prepares for the irony of the next verse, where the ones who set the trap are the ones caught in it.
17.explain:
“Surely, in vain the net is spread”

The father turns to a picture from bird-catching. A fowler spread a net to trap birds, usually hidden and baited so the bird would not notice it until too late. Spreading the net in vain means wasting the effort, because the bird is not caught.

“In the sight of any bird;”

The reason the effort is wasted is that the bird sees the net being spread. A bird that watches the trap being set has sense enough to avoid it. The point is driven home in the next verse: the gang is less sensible than a bird. They are setting a trap, but they cannot see that it is closing on themselves. The saying also carries a quiet warning to the son. He has now seen the net spread before his eyes, for the father has exposed the gang’s plan in full. If he walks into it now, he will have less sense than a bird.
17.notes:
The meaning of this saying is debated. Many take it as above: a bird avoids a net it sees, but the gang does not. Others read it as a bird that sees the net and still flies into it for the bait, so that even plain warning does not stop the greedy. A third view applies it to the son, who has been warned and should not be caught. On each reading 1:18 makes the same point.

The Hebrew word translated “in vain” is the same word rendered “without cause” in 1:11. The gang attacks the innocent for nothing, and their own net is spread for nothing.

18.brief: The gang thinks it is setting an ambush for the innocent, but they “lie in wait for their own blood.” Their violence will turn back on them, and the trap they lay for others becomes the trap that takes their own lives.
18.explain:
“But they lie in wait for their own blood,”

The verse repeats the gang’s own words from 1:11, “lie in wait” and “lurk secretly,” and turns them back on them. They thought they were setting an ambush for the innocent, but the ambush is really set for their own blood. They do not intend this; it is the outcome their path produces. In God’s ordered world, violence comes home to those who practice it.

“They lurk secretly for their own lives.”

The second line repeats the point with the second verb of 1:11. The secrecy they relied on will not protect them, and the lives they put at risk are their own. The psalmist describes the same pattern: “He made a pit and dug it out, And has fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psalm 7:15). The father has answered the gang’s offer of easy wealth by showing where it ends.
18.notes: Proverbs states the same principle in 26:27: “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, And he who rolls a stone will have it roll back on him.”

19.brief: The father draws the principle from the whole scene: this is the way of everyone who is greedy for gain. Greed takes away the life of its owners, so the wealth they would kill to get ends up killing them.
19.explain:
“So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain;”

“So” introduces the conclusion the father draws from the whole scene. He widens the lesson from this one gang to everyone who is greedy for gain. The phrase describes gain gotten by wrong means, profit that comes from cutting corners or taking what belongs to others. Most people tempted by greed will never join a band of robbers, but the same desire drives the cheat, the extortioner, and the dishonest businessman. The word ways is plural, pointing to a whole manner of life rather than a single act.

“It takes away the life of its owners.”

The gain itself turns on those who possess it. They think they own their wealth, but in the end it owns them, and it takes their lives. This may happen through violent retribution, as with the gang, or through the slower ruin that greed works in a person’s soul and relationships. Paul warns similarly that the desire to be rich leads into “many foolish and harmful lusts which drown men in destruction and perdition” (1 Timothy 6:9). The father’s first lesson ends with a principle his son can carry into every area of life.
19.notes:
In Hebrew, “greedy for gain” pairs a verb and a noun built from the same root, an expression that recurs in 15:27. The noun refers to gain gotten unjustly rather than to honest profit.

The Hebrew word translated “owners” is the plural of baal, a word for a lord or master. Those who think of themselves as masters of their gain lose their lives to it.

20.brief: A second voice now rises against the gang’s whispers: Wisdom, pictured as a woman, calls aloud outside and raises her voice in the open squares. She speaks where everyone passes, and in the fuller light of the New Testament this is the voice of Christ, the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24).
20.explain:
“Wisdom calls aloud outside;”

A second voice now rises against the gang’s whispers. Wisdom is pictured as a woman who speaks in person. The gang lurked in secret; Wisdom calls aloud outside, in the open, where anyone can hear. The Hebrew noun for wisdom is feminine, and the poem gives her a woman’s voice. This is personification, a poetic portrait of wisdom as a living person who calls, rebukes, warns, and promises.

“She raises her voice in the open squares.”

The open squares were the broad public places of a town, crowded with people buying, selling, and talking. Wisdom does not hide in a temple court or a scholar’s room. She raises her voice where ordinary people spend their days, and she sounds like one of Israel’s prophets standing in the street. Read in the fuller light of the New Testament, this voice is the voice of Christ, whom Paul calls “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), the One “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). That identification rests on the New Testament’s testimony rather than on the personification itself, since Folly is also pictured as a woman who calls (9:13–16). The feminine form belongs to the poem’s language; Wisdom is neither a goddess nor a picture of Christ as feminine. Jesus Himself spoke of “the wisdom of God” sending prophets (Luke 11:49).
20.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “Wisdom” here is in a plural form, yet the verb with it is singular, so one speaker is in view. The same form appears in 9:1. The plural probably expresses the fullness of wisdom; KJV’s margin explains it as “Excellent wisdom.”

The Hebrew verb translated “calls aloud” usually describes a ringing shout, often of joy. Here it describes a loud public cry that summons people to listen.

21.brief: She cries out in the busiest places, the main streets and the openings of the city gates, where trade was done and cases were judged. Wisdom’s call reaches people in the middle of ordinary public life, not only in sacred places.
21.explain:
“She cries out in the chief concourses,”

The chief concourses are the busiest places in town, the heads of the crowded and noisy streets. Wisdom goes where the crowds are thickest and lifts her voice above the din of trade and conversation.

“At the openings of the gates in the city”

The city gate was the center of public life in an ancient Israelite town. Elders sat there to judge cases and witness agreements (Ruth 4:1–2), merchants traded there, and news passed through it. By speaking at the gates, Wisdom places her call in the middle of commerce, law, and daily decision. Her counsel concerns the very matters settled in those places, such as honest dealing, fair judgment, and the choice of companions.

“She speaks her words:”

The colon introduces her speech, which runs to the end of the chapter (1:22–33). These are deliberate words, sayings meant to be heard and remembered. The contrast with the gang is complete: they whispered a plan of secret violence, while Wisdom speaks openly to anyone who will stop and listen.
21.notes:
ESV and the 1984 NIV render the first line as the head of the “noisy streets,” and NASB reads “noisy [streets],” bracketing the noun to show that it is supplied. NKJV has “chief concourses.” The Hebrew has a word meaning noisy or bustling, and the streets are understood.

Wisdom’s public call is repeated in 8:1–3, where she stands where the paths meet and cries out by the gates and at the entrance of the doors.

22.brief: Wisdom’s speech begins with a prophet’s lament: “How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity?” She addresses three kinds of people the book will develop: the simple, who are content to stay uncommitted; scorners, who enjoy mocking; and fools, who hate knowledge.
22.explain:
“How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity?”

Wisdom’s speech opens with a lament that sounds like Israel’s prophets. Elijah asked the people, “How long will you falter between two opinions?” (1 Kings 18:21). The simple are the uncommitted, and Wisdom’s charge is that they love being that way. Their danger is not open rebellion but contentment with drifting. They like keeping their options open and avoiding the commitment wisdom requires. “How long” implies that the time of drifting has already gone on too long.

“For scorners delight in their scorning,”

The scorner is a mocker who enjoys ridiculing correction and the people who give it. His problem is a matter of the will: the fool may lack sense, but the scorner refuses to be wise. He delights in his scorning, finding pleasure in contempt. Proverbs will later describe him as unteachable, the person who will not listen to rebuke (9:7–8; 13:1).

“And fools hate knowledge.”

The fool goes further than indifference: he hates knowledge. The three types move from loving simplicity, to delighting in mockery, to hating knowledge, which suggests how a person can harden over time. Wisdom addresses all three in one appeal. None of them is beyond her call while she is still calling.
22.notes: In Hebrew the question “How long” is asked once, at the start of the verse, but it carries through all three lines, and ESV repeats it before the scoffers. Where NKJV begins the second line with “For,” the Hebrew has only the ordinary word for “and”; NKJV’s choice presents the second line as an explanation of the first.

23.brief: Wisdom calls them to turn at her rebuke and promises that if they do, she will pour out her spirit on them and make her words known. In context she offers her own mind and teaching to those who turn, and her wording anticipates the LORD’s later promise to pour out His Spirit (Joel 2:28).
23.explain:
“Turn at my rebuke;”

Wisdom’s appeal now becomes a call to turn. To turn is to change direction, to leave the way one is walking and come back. The turning is at her rebuke, in response to her correction. This is exactly what the simple, the scorners, and the fools have refused to do, and it is the one thing that would change everything for them.

“Surely I will pour out my spirit on you;”

To those who turn, Wisdom makes a generous promise. To pour out is to give freely and abundantly, like water gushing from a spring. In context the spirit she promises is her own mind and heart, the inner life of wisdom given to those who listen, and NKJV’s lowercase spirit reflects that sense. The wording anticipates the LORD’s later promise through Joel, “I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28). Scripture as a whole draws that connection, and at Pentecost Peter said that the exalted Christ “poured out this which you now see and hear” (Acts 2:33). The verse is not a direct prediction of Pentecost. Yet when Wisdom’s voice is heard in the New Testament’s light as the voice of Christ, the One who calls people to turn is also the One who gives His Spirit to those who come.

“I will make my words known to you.”

The promise is also one of understanding. Wisdom will make her words known, opening their meaning to those who turn. Those who receive correction are the ones to whom more is revealed. The promise depends on the turning; Wisdom does not pour out her spirit on those who keep walking away.
23.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “pour out” pictures water bubbling up from a spring. Proverbs uses it of speech elsewhere: the mouth of fools “pours forth foolishness” (15:2), and a related form describes the wellspring of wisdom as a “flowing brook” (18:4).

24.brief: Wisdom’s tone turns to warning, and she gives the reason: she called, and they refused; she stretched out her hand, and no one paid attention. The outstretched hand pictures an earnest, personal appeal that was ignored.
24.explain:
“Because I have called and you refused,”

Wisdom’s tone turns from appeal to warning. The word “Because” begins an indictment that runs through 1:25, followed by the consequences in 1:26–27. She speaks as though a long season of refusal already lies behind her hearers. She called, and they refused. Refusal is an active choice, not mere inattention.

“I have stretched out my hand and no one regarded,”

An outstretched hand is a gesture of earnest, personal appeal, the hand held out to draw someone near or to rescue him. The LORD uses the same language of His own pleading with Israel: “I have stretched out My hands all day long to a rebellious people” (Isaiah 65:2). Wisdom’s call was not cold or distant. She reached out, and no one paid attention. Their guilt lies in ignoring a hand that was truly offered.
24.notes: Wisdom’s words closely resemble the LORD’s indictment in Isaiah 65:12: “Because, when I called, you did not answer; When I spoke, you did not hear.” Compare also Isaiah 66:4 and Jeremiah 7:13.

25.brief: They did more than ignore her, for they disdained all her counsel and wanted none of her rebuke. Their refusal was a settled choice to reject both her guidance and her correction.
25.explain:
“Because you disdained all my counsel,”

The indictment continues. To disdain her counsel is to let it go, to treat it as of no account. Counsel is guidance, the advice that would have shown them the right way. They disdained all of it; nothing she offered was received. The word all stresses that the refusal was complete.

“And would have none of my rebuke,”

Rebuke is correction, the word that exposes wrong and calls for change. These hearers did not want it at all. Rejecting counsel is refusing to be guided; rejecting rebuke is refusing to be corrected. Together they describe people who will neither be led nor turned back. The same pair returns in 1:30, showing that this was their settled pattern.
25.notes:
“Would have none” translates the same Hebrew verb as “Do not consent” in 1:10, a verb meaning to be willing. The son is told not to be willing toward sinners; these hearers were not willing toward Wisdom.

Where NKJV has “disdained,” KJV says the hearers set Wisdom’s counsel at nought.

26.brief: Because they mocked her, Wisdom says she will laugh at their calamity and mock when their terror comes. This is the language of judgment, turning the scorners’ own mockery back on them; it does not picture Wisdom delighting in suffering.
26.explain:
“I also will laugh at your calamity;”

The word also marks a correspondence. The scorners delighted in their scorning (1:22), and now their mockery is turned back on them. Wisdom’s laughter is the language of judgment, the same language used of the LORD in the face of rebellion: “He who sits in the heavens shall laugh” (Psalm 2:4). It declares that opposition to God’s wisdom is futile and that those who mocked it will be exposed. It does not picture Wisdom taking pleasure in pain. The LORD says, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11), and Jesus wept over the city that would not come to Him (Luke 19:41).

“I will mock when your terror comes,”

Their terror is the disaster they dread. When it comes, the people who laughed at Wisdom will find that their own scorn has returned to them. The warning is severe because the stakes are real. Wisdom says these words while she is still calling, and the warning is meant to turn people before the calamity arrives.
26.notes: The Hebrew word for “terror” returns in 1:27 and again in 1:33, where whoever listens to Wisdom lives “without fear of evil,” using the same noun. The terror that comes on those who refuse is set against the security of those who listen.

27.brief: The calamity arrives suddenly and overwhelmingly, like a storm and a whirlwind, bringing distress and anguish. The images show that the consequences of refusing wisdom do not come gently or on the sinner’s schedule.
27.explain:
“When your terror comes like a storm,”

Wisdom describes the calamity in images of violent weather. A storm comes with sudden force, and nothing a person has built can stand before it. The disaster that follows refusing wisdom is not gentle, and it does not wait for a convenient time.

“And your destruction comes like a whirlwind,”

The whirlwind is a storm wind that sweeps everything away. The gang boasted that they would swallow others whole (1:12); now those who refuse Wisdom are swept away themselves. Proverbs uses the same picture later: “When the whirlwind passes by, the wicked is no more” (10:25).

“When distress and anguish come upon you.”

Distress and anguish describe pressure and constriction, the feeling of being hemmed in with no way out. The word “comes” is repeated through the verse, and the effect is of disaster arriving wave upon wave. The verse completes the sentence begun in 1:26: when all this comes, Wisdom will not rescue those who refused her.
27.notes: The two Hebrew nouns behind “distress and anguish” sound alike (tsarah and tsuqah), and the matching sounds add force to the line.

28.brief: Wisdom now speaks of them rather than to them: in their trouble they will call on her and seek her diligently, but she will not answer, and they will not find her. Seeking her only to escape disaster, after a long refusal, comes too late to turn back the consequences they chose.
28.explain:
“Then they will call on me, but I will not answer;”

Wisdom now speaks about her hearers rather than to them, as if turning from them to address the crowd. In their distress they will call on her, the very thing she begged them to do while she was calling. Now she will not answer. They are seeking relief from the consequences, not Wisdom herself.

“They will seek me diligently, but they will not find me.”

Even earnest seeking will fail at that point. The verse does not say that a person who turns to God can never be heard. Scripture calls people to “Seek the LORD while He may be found” (Isaiah 55:6), and the very purpose of this warning is to bring people to seek while the door is open. What the verse describes is the end of a long refusal. When the harvest of rejected wisdom arrives, crying out for help does not undo what a person has sown. No one who turns to the Lord in repentance should read this verse as a sentence that it is too late for him; the warning is given so that it will not be.
28.notes:
The Hebrew verb in “seek me diligently” is built from the noun for dawn, and its older sense was probably looking for the dawn, or being up early. That is why KJV translates the line with the word “early.” Modern versions take it as earnest, diligent seeking.

The shift from “you” in 1:22–27 to “they” in 1:28–32 marks the change from direct appeal to a description of what will happen to those who refuse.

29.brief: The reason is stated plainly: they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD. Their ruin was no accident, for at its root was a refusal to see God rightly and live before Him.
29.explain:
“Because they hated knowledge”

Wisdom gives the reason for their end. They hated knowledge, which echoes her description of the fools in 1:22. Their problem was never a lack of information or opportunity. They disliked the truth that would have corrected them.

“And did not choose the fear of the LORD,”

The fear of the LORD is presented as something a person chooses. Those who perish did not choose it; they preferred their own way to a right view of God. This takes the reader straight back to the motto in 1:7. Knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD, and ruin follows when a person refuses it. Wisdom’s speech also shows that rejecting her is the same as rejecting the LORD Himself, for her counsel and the fear of the LORD go together. The verse places responsibility squarely on those who refused.
29.notes: “The fear of the LORD” appears in 1:7 and again in 1:29, so that the chapter’s argument is enclosed between the beginning of knowledge and the refusal that leads to ruin.

30.brief: Wisdom repeats the charge: they would have none of her counsel and despised every rebuke she gave. The repetition stresses that they were not left without warning; they were corrected again and again and refused each time.
30.explain:
“They would have none of my counsel”

Wisdom repeats the charge of 1:25 almost word for word. The repetition is deliberate. These people were not left without warning or without guidance. Counsel was offered, and they would have none of it.

“And despised my every rebuke.”

To despise is to treat with contempt. This is stronger than the disdain of 1:25, and it was their response to every rebuke, not just one. Correction came again and again, and each time it was spurned. When the end comes, they cannot claim that no one told them. The verse closes the case Wisdom has been building since 1:24.

31.brief: Therefore they will eat the fruit of their own way and be filled to the full with their own fancies. No new punishment needs to be invented, for the schemes they preferred become the harvest they must eat.
31.explain:
“Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their own way,”

“Therefore” brings the conclusion. The judgment Wisdom announces is that they will eat the fruit of their own way. No new punishment has to be invented; the choices they made produce their own harvest. A person who chooses a way chooses its destination. This principle runs throughout Scripture: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). The word way connects the verse with the road picture of 1:15 and 1:19.

“And be filled to the full with their own fancies.”

Their fancies are their schemes, their own plans and ideas about how to live. They refused Wisdom’s counsel and preferred their own; now they will have all of their own they can stomach, and more. To be filled to the full is to be glutted. The gang hoped to fill their houses with spoil (1:13). Those who refuse Wisdom are filled as well, with the bitter results of their own devices.
31.notes: NKJV’s “fancies” translates a Hebrew word meaning plans or schemes; KJV and ESV render it “devices.” It comes from the same root as the word for “counsel” in 1:25 and 1:30, so those who rejected Wisdom’s counsel are filled with counsels of their own.

32.brief: Wisdom names two ways people perish: the simple are slain by their turning away, and fools are destroyed by their complacency. Neither needs open rebellion to be lost, since drifting from wisdom and careless ease are deadly enough.
32.explain:
“For the turning away of the simple will slay them,”

Wisdom names two ways people perish. The first is the turning away of the simple. Wisdom called them to turn at her rebuke (1:23); instead they turned away. The simple do not have to rebel openly to be lost. Drifting away from wisdom, a little at a time and without settled commitment, is enough to kill them. That is why the book is so urgent for the simple, who are always open to the next voice.

“And the complacency of fools will destroy them;”

The second way is the complacency of fools. Complacency is careless ease, a false sense of security that assumes nothing bad will happen. Fools feel comfortable, and their comfort is what destroys them. Neither line describes a dramatic act of defiance. One is drift and the other is ease, and both are deadly. The danger in each is that it does not feel like danger to the person in it.
32.notes:
The Hebrew noun for “turning away” comes from the verb translated “Turn” in 1:23. Jeremiah uses it for Israel’s backsliding: “Return, you backsliding children, And I will heal your backslidings” (Jeremiah 3:22).

KJV renders “complacency” as “prosperity.” The Hebrew word describes ease or quiet, and here the context shows a careless ease.

33.brief: The speech ends with hope: whoever listens to Wisdom will dwell safely and be secure, without fear of evil. This is the general truth of the wise way, a security that rests on hearing her, set against the ruin just described.
33.explain:
“But whoever listens to me will dwell safely,”

Wisdom’s speech ends with hope. The way out of all she has described is simple: listen to her. To listen is to hear and heed, the same response the wise man gives in 1:5 and the son is asked to give in 1:8. Whoever listens, whether simple, young, or long resistant, will dwell safely. The promise is open to anyone.

“And will be secure, without fear of evil.”

The listener will be secure, at ease, undisturbed by the terror that sweeps over those who refuse Wisdom (1:26–27). This is a different kind of ease from the complacency of fools in 1:32. Theirs was false security that ignored danger; this is true security that rests on hearing wisdom. Like the rest of Proverbs, the line states what is generally true of the wise way, not a promise that the wise will never suffer. The deepest security this line promises is found in the One whom Wisdom pictures. Jesus said, “My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me” (John 10:27).
33.notes: The promise of security is developed in 3:23–26, where the son who keeps wisdom is told, “Do not be afraid of sudden terror” (3:25).
